Apple's candle is in a silver holder. Samsung’s candle was previously pink, perhaps as in a birthday cake.

A light bulb, as screwed into a lamp to light a room. Depicted as an incandescent bulb with a silver base, often shown with filament and a soft, yellow-white glow.

Commonly used to represent ideas (as over a head in a cartoon), thinking, and learning, often as paired with 🤔 Thinking Face or 💭 Thought Balloon. May also represent various senses of light and brightness.

An everyday flashlight (electric torch), as used when the power goes out, camping, or telling scary stories. Generally depicted at a 45° angle as a gray and black device with a switch, shown illuminated on many platforms.

Used for various content concerning and senses of light and lighting, both literal and metaphorical. Beyond representing a handheld torch, it is also used to represent different kinds of stage and ambient lighting, including spotlights, mood lighting. In extended or figurative contexts, it may symbolize revealing, investigating, examining, or "shining a light" on something.

Google’s flashlight was previously orange.

A locked (closed) padlock, as used to secure a latch or chain, or as an icon for a secure internet connection, private account, or locked device. Generally depicted with a gold base and silver shackle. WhatsApp’s design is silver.

Commonly used for content concerning safety, security, privacy, and protection as well as various senses of lock, e.g., locked in/down. As such, it can be used to encapsulate the slang phrase “locked in,” to convey intense focus, commitment, or full mental engagement on a task or goal.

This emoji does not display in page titles on Apple’s Safari web browser, presumably to prevent less reputable sites from pretending to be secure (encrypted using HTTPS).

Additionally, this emoji is not supported in Twitter / X names, to minimize confusion with private accounts on the platform. Learn more here.

See also: 🔏 Locked With Pen and 🔐 Locked With Key.

An unlocked padlock, as used to secure a latch or chain, or as an icon for a non-secure connection or open access online. Generally depicted with a gold base and silver shackle, as an open 🔒 Locked.

May be used to represent a lack of or concerns about privacy and security. May also be used for figurative senses of unlocking, e.g., achievement unlocked.

WhatsApp’s design is silver, its shackle turned to the right, as Samsung’s previously was.

This emoji does not display in page titles on Apple’s Safari web browser, presumably to prevent less reputable sites from pretending to be secure (encrypted using HTTPS).

Additionally, this emoji is not supported in Twitter / X names, to minimize confusion with private accounts on the platform. Learn more here.

A locked (closed) padlock with a fountain pen or nib positioned at various angles in front of it. Vendors implement the same design as their 🔒 Locked and the same or similar design as their 🖋 Fountain Pen or ✒ Black Nib.

May represent digital certificates in public-key technology. May also have similar applications as 🔒 Locked (privacy, security) and 🖋 Fountain Pen or ✒ Black Nib (writing, signing).

It can also be used to encapsulate the slang phrase “locked in,” to convey intense focus, commitment, or full mental engagement on a task or goal.

Apple’s design previously displayed a nib, as did Google’s.

This emoji does not display in page titles on Apple’s Safari web browser, presumably to prevent less reputable sites from pretending to be secure (encrypted using HTTPS).

Additionally, this emoji is not supported in Twitter / X names, to minimize confusion with private accounts on the platform. Learn more here.

A locked (closed) padlock with an upright key at its right. Vendors implement the same designs as their 🔒 Locked and 🔑 Key.

May represent digital keys in public-key technology. May have similar applications as 🔒 Locked (privacy, security) and 🔑 Key (means of access, "crucial"). Sometimes used to represent a locket to symbolize romantic love and commitment.

It can also be used to encapsulate the slang phrase “locked in,” to convey intense focus, commitment, or full mental engagement on a task or goal.

Apple’s design previously featured the easter egg UM242 on its key, a reference to locks on Herman Miller office furniture. Facebook’s design once displayed a silver key, its head at the bottom.

This emoji does not display in page titles on Apple’s Safari web browser, presumably to prevent less reputable sites from pretending to be secure (encrypted using HTTPS).

Additionally, this emoji is not supported in Twitter / X names, to minimize confusion with private accounts on the platform. Learn more here.

A key, as opens a door or lock. Depicted at a 45° angle as a gold, bronze, or copper key with a round head and notched blade. Commonly used for figurative senses of key, e.g., the key to success, being key ("crucial").

DJ Khaled uses the emoji to indicate his Snapchat stories are official (verified). Apple’s design previously resembled a gold 🗝 Old Key, which emoji has similar applications.

May also represent digital keys in public-key technology. This may explain why the emoji does not display in page titles on Apple’s Safari web browser, presumably to prevent less reputable sites from pretending to be secure (encrypted using HTTPS).

An old-fashioned key, as opens an antique chest or wardrobe. Generally depicted at a 45° angle as a tarnished, silver skeleton key with an ornate, bowed head and two-toothed bit at the bottom left.

Like 🔑 Key, often used figuratively, e.g., the key to success, being key ("crucial"). May also be applied to antiques.

Microsoft’s design is gold, with the head at the upper left. Samsung and Facebook’s keys were previously gold.

A claw hammer, as used for driving or removing nails. Generally depicted with a metal head and wooden handle, positioned at a 45° angle with the head at the upper left.

Commonly used for content concerning tools, building, and construction as well as various senses of breaking or smashing. May also represent hard work or be applied to hammer-related expressions, e.g., nailed it.

Apple and Facebook’s designs previously displayed a gavel, Softbank’s a mallet. Not to be confused with ⛏ Pick or 🪓 Axe.
An axe with a wooden handle and a metal blade. On many platforms the blade is red, like a fire axe.

A hammer and wrench, as kept in a toolbox, crossed in an X shape. Depicted with metal tools facing up, the hammer positioned at the upper left. Most vendors implement the same design as for their 🔨 Hammer and 🔧 Wrench.

Commonly used for various content concerning tools, building, construction, and work, both manual and digital.

A pointed knife with a steel blade, as used for thrusting in close combat. Generally depicted as double-edged with a black, brown or gold cross-shaped hilt and positioned at 45° angle, often with its tip at the lower left.

May represent knives and other bladed weapons (cf. ⚔ Crossed Swords) as well as various senses of cutting and stabbing. Often applied to medieval or fantasy content.

Google’s design previously featured an icy-blue blade and sparkles, suggests a dagger elves may wield in fantasy.

May be paired with (or defended by) 🛡 Shield. Not to be confused with 🔪 Kitchen Knife.

A cartoon-styled bomb, depicted as a black ball with a burning fuse.

Commonly used for various figurative bombs or explosions, e.g., slang bomb, a “home run” in baseball or softball; "excellent" or "attractive." Sometimes applied in contexts of war, weapons, or violence.

Earlier designs from SoftBank and au by KDDI animated the bomb as exploding.

A wooden boomerang with bright colors on its tips. Google and Twitter's designs show motion lines to illustrate the path of a boomerang.

Used literally to represent a boomerang. Also used to represent Aboriginal people or Australia in general. May be used to represent something that comes back or returns.

A bow and arrow used in the sport of archery. May also be used by cupid.

Can also be used to represent ♐ Sagittarius in the Western zodiac.

A shield, as blocks swords in close combat. Color and style varies across platforms, but generally depicted in a kite shape with a metal border and simple pattern.

Commonly used to represent various content concerning battle, defense, security, and protection.

Apple and Microsoft’s designs feature a red and white sawtooth pattern, Facebook and WhatsApp’s blue and white checkers.

May be paired with (or fending off) ⚔ Crossed Swords or 🗡 Dagger. Not to be confused with 🔰 Japanese Symbol for Beginner.
A long silver saw with a wooden handle. Used to represent construction, carpentry, renovation, or tools in general.

A metal wrench (spanner), as used for turning nuts and bolts. Depicted with two open, crescent-shaped ends or one open end and a closed, ring-shaped end. Generally positioned at a 45° angle.

Commonly used for various content concerning tools, building, maintenance, and skilled trades like car mechanics and plumbing.

A silver Phillips-head or slotted-head screwdriver with a colorful handle. Most platforms show a red handle, though Apple's design has a green handle. Used to represent construction, building, carpentry, renovation, or tools in general.

Sometimes used in phrases with 'screw' in them like screw you or have a screw loose. Can also be used in sexual contexts due to the informal meaning of 'screw': "to have sex."

A metal bolt with a nut threaded around it, as by a wrench. Often positioned at a 45° angle, the head of the bolt at the upper left. Commonly used for various content concerning tools, building, and construction. May also be used for other hardware, including screws.

Apple’s bolt previously resembled a screw, Google’s a dumbbell; Microsoft’s design previously featured the nut and bolt separately.

A metal clamp or vice, as screwed to hold or compress materials like wood or metal. Depicted as a C-clamp or F-clamp, its screw in various positions.

Commonly used for various content concerning tools, equipment, and technology. May also represent file compression in computer science. An image of a clamp, for example, is featured in the WinZip icon.

Twitter’s clamp is red. Samsung’s design previously featured a clamp around a cardboard box.

Two links of a silver chain, positioned at a 45° angle. Used as an icon for a hyperlink on computers and the internet. May also be used for metaphorical connections.

Not to be confused with ⛓Chains, 📎 Paperclip, 🖇 Linked Paperclips, or 🧷 Safety Pin.

A single length of metal chain that has had one of its links forcefully broken apart. Usually displayed with emphasis marks around the fracture point.

Can be used to discuss freedom and liberty, as well as various types of malfunction.

A gold or silver hook. Can be used to represent literal hooks like the kinds you use to crochet or catch fish.

Also use metaphorically to talk about boxing or punching, music (the catchy part of a song), or in phrases like hook me up, hook up, getting hooked (on something), or hook, line, and sinker.

A red box for holding and transporting tools, such as a hammer and wrench. Generally depicted as latched shut with silver hardware and a black handle.

Commonly used for literal or metaphorical tools, toolkits, and building.

WhatsApp's design includes a hammer in front. Google’s design was previously shown as open with two wrenches and a pair of pliers.

A horseshoe magnet, as used to pick up iron. Depicted at various angles in red with silver-tipped poles.

Commonly used for various content concerning literal and figurative magnetism and attraction. May also be used in various science-related contexts more generally.

Twitter’s design features two electric bolts coming from its poles. WhatsApp’s horseshoe is half blue, denoting an opposite magnetic pole.

A wooden ladder with four or five rungs.

Used to represent ladders or the action of climbing. Also used metaphorically to represent systems through which you can climb, for example the corporate ladder or social ladder.
A tool used to move loose material such as sand, coal, or snow.

A test tube, as used to conduct chemical experiments in a laboratory. Depicted as a clear cylinder, open at one end and containing a green liquid. Positioned at a 45° angle.

May be used for various content concerning chemistry and science more generally. May also represent other liquids, such as potions or medicines, as well metaphorical laboratories and experiments.

Some platforms include volume markings or display the liquid as bubbling. WhatsApp’s design features a blue liquid.

A petri dish, as used to culture microbes. Depicted as a clear, shallow cylinder with a red, blue, or green growth medium, such as agar, with splotches of variously colored cells, like bacteria.

May be used for various content concerning biology and science more generally. May also be used to represent germs and other microorganisms.

Samsung’s design features a lid, while Google’s design previously featured a dropper.

A microscope, as used in science laboratories to magnify small objects, such as cells or insects. Depicted as a compound opitical microscope with an adjustable eyepiece, lens, arm, and slide stage mounted on a base. Generally shown as metal with the viewing apparatus facing left.

Commonly used for various content concerning science and research. May also be used for various senses of inspection (e.g., taking a closer took).

Google’s design was previously shown in red.

A telescope, as used to gaze at stars and planets in the night sky. Shown with an optical tube mounted on a tripod, positioned at various angles and generally depicted as metal.

Commonly used for various content concerning astronomy, outer space, celestial objects, and science more generally. May also be used for various concepts of sight (e.g., spying, viewing).

Twitter’s designs feature red hardware, as did as an older Google design.

A dish antenna, as used to send or receive information to or from a communication satellite—or 👽 Extraterrestrial Life. Generally depicted as a mounted, metal dish with its antenna positioned at 45° to the upper right.

Commonly used to represent satellite television, radio, and internet, as well as broadcasting, streaming, cellular, and wireless services or technologies. May also represent various concepts of signals and transmission.

Several platforms, including Microsoft and Twitter, feature curved, radiating lines, as if transmitting data.

A medical syringe, as used to administer a vaccine or draw blood. Generally depicted at a 45° angle with a needle to the upper right.

Commonly used for content concerning health, medicine, and related professions as well as various senses of needles, drugs, tattoos, blood, or more recently – coronavirus vaccination.

Originally used for the representation of blood donation, and displayed with blood in the barrel. In 2021 many platforms are switching to a more general-purpose empty syringe. Google and Facebook’s designs previously featured green liquids.
An adhesive bandage used for first aid. Sometimes called a Band-Aid or band aid after the trademarked product. Sometimes called a plaster.
A basic crutch made of metal and rubber.
A stethoscope with a round resonator and two earpieces. Shown in black, blue, green, or red, depending on the platform.

An X-ray image. Most designs show a human thorax (including the rib cage and shoulder blades).

Microsoft shows a skull, while X's design shows a hand.

May be used to talk about X-rays or medicine in general.

A door, as to the entrance of a room, house, or new opportunity. (We’ll see ourselves out 🚪🚶) Depicted in brown, as made of wood, with a gold handle.

May represent literal doors and related concepts (e.g., rooms, houses) but often used figuratively (e.g., opening or closing metaphorical doors).

Microsoft’s design previously featured a step, as if a front door. Google’s design previously featured a peephole.

A mirror with an ornate gold or silver frame. The shape and style of the mirror varies from platform to platform.

Used to talk about mirrors, reflection, or self-reflection.

A square or rectangular window with glass panes. Most platforms show a wooden frame with two or four panels.

Used to talk about actual windows or metaphorical windows, which often represent opportunities, perspectives, or unique points of view.

A bed, made up for sleeping in a house, hotel, or other sleeping accommodation. Shown with a headboard at the left, footboard, mattress, pillow, and sheet. Most platforms suggest a wooden frame and feature blue or red sheets.

Commonly used for various content concerning beds, furniture, and housing as well as sleeping, relaxing, and other bedroom activities.

Vendors implement the same style of bed for 🛌 Person in Bed, but without a sleeper under the covers.

A couch (sofa) with a floor lamp on the right, as in the living room of a house. Color and style of the couch and lamp vary widely by platform. Used for various content concerning furniture and housing as well as resting and lounging.

Distinct from 💺 Seat, which is generally depicted as a fixed plane, train, or bus seat, as opposed to a chair which can be moved.

May have sexual connotations (e.g., sit on my face).

In 2021 this emoji was also used on TikTok to signify laughter or approval or to create confusion for people not in the know. Learn more here.

A white toilet, as used to deposit a 💩 Pile of Poo. (Don’t forget the 🧻 Roll of Paper.) Most platforms depict a porcelain toilet in profile, bowl facing to the left.

Commonly used for various content concerning going to the bathroom or bathrooms more generally. May also be used figuratively, e.g., down the toilet.

Google, Microsoft, and Twitter’s designs left the seat up.

A toilet plunger with a wooden handle and red flange and cup.

Used to talk about toilets and clogged pipes. Also used metaphorically to talk about a mess or something that's disgusting.

A silver shower head, streaming water to the left. Pressure level varies across platforms. 🧼 Soap not provided.

Commonly used for various content concerning bathing, washing, cleaning, and water. Shower heads are also featured in 🛁 Bathtub and 🛀 Person Taking a Bath.

A white bathtub with a silver shower head. Often depicted as a cast-iron tub with claw-foot legs. Commonly used for various content concerning bathing, washing, cleaning, and bathrooms more generally.

Several platforms, including Apple and Facebook, feature soap bubbles or suds. Samsung’s design displays streaming water from the shower head.

Vendors implement 🛀 Person Taking a Bath with the same or a similar emoji, but with a person soaking in the tub.

A trap used to catch a mouse, rat, or other unwanted rodent. Metaphorically used in emoji form to suggest any kind of trap or entrapment.

The style of trap shown on major platforms has a box held high with a single stick. A wedge of cheese is used to lure a mouse into the box, knocking the stick away and trapping — but not killing — the mouse.

This is distinct from other traps which kill or injure upon capture.

A safety razor, depicted in various colors across platforms.

Previously shown as a straight razor by Microsoft, WhatsApp, and JoyPixels.

A bottle of lotion for the skin, such as moisturizer or sunscreen (sunblock). May be used for other hygienic liquids, including shampoo and body wash, as well as beauty products.

Appearance varies across platforms, but commonly depicted in white and gold colors. Some designs also include a droplet icon on the bottle.

Most platforms feature a bottle with a pump, though others previously displayed a cylinder with a cap.

A silver safety pin or clip, as used to fasten fabric. Generally shown clasped at a 45° angle, with its spring at the lower left.

May be used for various content concerning arts, crafts, and sewing. Not to be confused with 📎 Paperclip.

A traditional broom, as used for sweeping—or ridden by a witch. Shown at a 45° angle, with a wooden handle and yellow bristles at the lower left.

Commonly used for various content concerning cleaning, brushing, and figurative sweeps (e.g., in sports or awards). Not to be confused with 🖌 Paintbrush.

A basket, as used for storing or carrying such things as food or clothes. Appearance widely varies across platforms but generally depicted as woven from wicker with one or more handles. Commonly used to represent doing laundry or having a picnic.

Apple and WhatsApp’s designs, featuring a white cloth, suggest a bread or picnic basket. Samsung’s design displays green fabric, as knitted from yarn.

Microsoft’s design previously suggested a laundry basket by holding a blue garment or cloth.

Not to be confused with 🗑 Wastebasket.

A roll of paper, as toilet paper (toilet tissue). May also be a roll of kitchen/paper towels. Depicted at various angles, with a sheet unfurling.

Commonly used for toilet paper but may also be used for various content concerning toilets, going to the bathroom, bathrooms, cleaning, or paper more generally.

A blue or green bucket or pail. Used to talk about real or metaphorical buckets.

May be used to talk about bucket lists, kicking the bucket, making baskets in basketball, an abundance of something (like rain or money), and many other contexts.

A bar of soap, as used in the shower, bath or for hand washing. Generally shown with lathered bubbles. Depicted in various colors, often pink, and at different angles.

Commonly used for various content concerning bathing, washing, and cleaning. May be used to represent the opposite of dirt or being dirty. Recommended for use to prevent the spread of COVID-19 and other illnesses.

May be used to encapsulate the slang term “washed,” meaning no longer effective or past one’s prime. Could also be used to refer to the slang term for money, including cash associated with bribery or illicit payments, referencing the concept of “washing” money.
A few floating bubbles. May be used to represent soap suds, carbonation, or an effervescent personality.

A brightly colored plastic toothbrush with white bristles.

Used to talk about oral hygiene, daily routines, or something that is fresh and clean.

A peanut-shaped sponge, as used for cleaning or bathing. Generally depicted in yellow and at different angles across platforms. Commonly used for various content concerning bathing, washing, and cleaning.

May also be used to evoke the metaphor of the brain as a sponge, absorbing knowledge or soaking up information.

A fire extinguisher, as used to put out small fires. Depicted as a red tank with a black hose and pressure gauge. Most platforms include an image of a flame on a white label.

Commonly used for various content concerning fire safety, emergencies, and literal and figurative fires.

A metal shopping cart that you might find in a supermarket or grocery store.

The color of the cart's wheels and handle vary by platform. Previous Google designs displayed the cart itself as yellow and orange, while Facebook's cart is red.

Most popular around Black Friday and into the Christmas season.

A lit, filtered cigarette, is shown burning at different directions. Commonly used to represent various forms of smoking (e.g., tobacco, marijuana, vaping) as well as metaphorical senses of smoking.

Can be used in reference to the 'I Haven't Heard That Name In Years' meme, which depicts a person or character smoking while recalling someone from their (often painful) past.

Originally intended as a sign for a designated smoking area, as contrasted to 🚭 No Smoking Symbol. This is illustrated in Samsung’s previous design of a stylized, white cigarette on a blue background.

A headstone or tombstone, used to mark graves. Appearance varies from platform to platform, with different shapes and inscriptions.

Used to talk about death — literally, metaphorically, and metaphysically.

Often paired with other death-related emoji like ⚰ Coffin and ☠ Skull and Crossbones.

A sign on a post, commonly used to promote ideas, causes, or make announcements. Often used used in the context of politics to represent a lawn sign or a poster brought to a protest. Also seen in commercial advertising.

Shown with indiscernible writing or not writing at all, this emoji is flexible in its use. WhatsApp shows a peace sign, which tilts the meaning away from commercial use.

A globe, showing the continents of Europe and Africa in green against blue ocean.

May be used to represent various content concerning the European, African, and Atlantic regions. May also be used to represent Earth and international affairs more generally.

See also 🌎 Globe Showing Americas and 🌏 Globe Showing Asia-Australia.

A globe, showing the continents of North and South America in green against blue ocean.

May be used to represent various content concerning the North and South American regions as well Atlantic and Pacific regions. May also be used to represent Earth and international affairs more generally.

See also 🌍 Globe Showing Europe-Africa and 🌏 Globe Showing Asia-Australia.

A globe, showing the continents of Asia and Australia in green against blue ocean.

May be used to represent various content concerning the Asian, Australian, and Pacific regions. May also be used to represent Earth and international affairs more generally.

See also 🌎 Globe Showing Americas and 🌍 Globe Showing Europe-Africa.

A stylized globe, with blue meridians (longitudes) and latitude. Depicted with light-blue grid of lines on a white, blue, or empty circle.

May be used as a symbol of the internet or world wide web, global communications, international affairs, connectivity and networks, time zones, coordinates, or the world more generally.

In political discourse, this emoji is sometimes used as shorthand for “globalism” or “globalist” viewpoints.

May appear as an icon on Apple devices to change (language) keyboards.

See also 🌎 Globe Showing Americas, 🌍 Globe Showing Europe-Africa, and 🌏 Globe Showing Asia-Australia.

A rectangular map of the world. Generally depicted as a paper map creased at its folds, Earth’s surface shown in green on blue ocean.

Commonly represent maps, travel, exploration, and geography. May also represent various content concerning the world as a whole, e.g., global or international issues.

Microsoft and Samsung’s design previously depicted outlines of the continents.
Shows a map of the country of Japan, which is the only country to have its own emoji map. Other countries can be found on the various globe emojis, or the world map emoji.

A magnetic compass, as used for navigation. Generally depicted in a silver or gold case with a compass rose and a red-tipped needle. Commonly used for various content concerning traveling and exploring as well as metaphorical compasses (e.g., moral compass).

Facebook’s markings include the initials of the four cardinal directions, north, south, east, and west. Not to be confused with various clock or timepiece emojis.
A mountain with snow resting at higher altitudes. Similar in appearance to the Mount Fuji emoji.
A cliff face with debris falling down its side, creating a potentially dangerous landslide.
A volcano, erupting with smoke and lava.

Mount Fuji (called Fuji-san in Japan) is the tallest mountain in Japan. Often seen with snow on the peak in colder months of the year.

Occasionally used to reference broad Japanese cultural themes, including by those vacationing in the country, but can also be used generally to represent mountains or scenic landscapes.

Similar to ⛰ Mountain and 🏔 Snow-Capped Mountain, it can also be used metaphorically to represent ambition, stability, or perseverance.

It is considered lucky in Japan to dream of Mt Fuji in the first dream of the new year.
A campsite featuring a tent and a tree, and perhaps a campfire. Similar to the tent emoji.

A beach showing sand, and an umbrella for protection from the sun.

This emoji tends to spike in popularity during the summer months.
A dry sand-covered desert. Generally depicted via a cactus and a large rock formation. Often also features a depiction of a blistering sun.

A small sand-covered island with a central palm tree. Occasionally also features a coconut or two.

During the summer of 2024 this emoji became associated with then-Vice President of the Untied States Kamala Harris, referencing a viral clip of a speech made in May 2023 where she stated: "You think you just fell out of a coconut tree? You exist in the context of all in which you live and what came before you.”

A national park, generally displayed with mountains, a river or stream, and trees.

Most often used in posts about nature, hiking, or travel. May also suggest peace, escape, or appreciation for natural beauty.
A large capacity stadium, featuring a large amount of seating for sporting fans, or people attending other shows hosted by the stadium.
A building shown with columns in a classical style, sometimes used to represent a courthouse, town hall, post office or stock exchange.
A construction site generally depicted as a tower crane shown lifting steel or other building materials.

A red brick or bricks. Depicted in a loose stack, a single object with holes, or as built into wall, as of a house, school, or other structure.

Commonly used for discussing building and construction. May also be used to reference blockades or obstructions, either literal or intangible.

It may also be used in further figurative contexts, such as describing extremely cold weather (“it’s brick”), a non-functional electronic device (“bricked”), or in sexual slang ("bricked up").
A round hut with a thatched roof. Used to talk about huts, cottages, yurts, or homes in general.

Multiple houses near one another.

May be used to discuss neighbourhoods, communities, or possibly real estate more broadly.

A house that is unoccupied and has fallen into disrepair, typically shown with boarded-up windows or doors.

Can be used to represent neglect or decay, and as such is often used to reference haunted houses, building restoration, or urban exploration.

May also be used metaphorically to express emotional neglect or feelings of abandonment.

A house, otherwise known as a home when someone is living in it. Suitable for a couple or larger family, other perhaps housemates.

Distinct from an apartment building due to its detached form, this house is likely in the suburbs of a city or a rural area.
A suburban-looking house, with a tree, flower, or shrubs around it in the garden.

A generic, high-rise office building, intended to represent workplaces, company headquarters, or urban business districts. Generally found in cities and most active during business hours.

The office building shown in Twemoji from 2015 onwards is the former Twitter HQ in San Francisco, located at Market Square.

A Japanese post office, featuring the 〒 Japanese postal mark on the front of the building.

Microsoft's design previously displayed this mark on its own instead of being featured on the building.
A European-style post office. A postal horn can be seen on the front, which is commonly found in the logos of European Postal Services.
A place where people are taken to receive medical care. This hospital has a large red cross on the front, often used as a symbol for health care.

A hotel building, displayed on most platforms as a building with many windows and a letter H on the front.

Can be easily confused with the Love Hotel, or Hospital emoji. Microsoft previously depicted this emoji as a bed.

A love hotel is a hotel that can be hired by the hour instead of as accommodation for the evening.

Sometimes mistaken for a get well soon emoji due to the similarity in appearance to the hospital. The Microsoft version of this emoji previously displaying a bed with a heart above it.

A shop that is generally open for longer hours than a regular supermarket, sometimes 24 hours per day.

Sells a range of goods from snacks, meals, hygiene products and household items.

A school building with multiple storeys, and a clock on the front. A place that children or teenagers attend for their education.

This emoji tends to spike in use in September when many Northern Hemisphere countries' schools reopen after their summer holidays.

Previously displayed on Windows as a collection of school-related items: an apple, ruler, and pencil.

A large department store, selling a range of products to the general public. Shown as a large building with a billboard.

Previously shown as a shopping bag on Windows.
An industrial factory, with flue-gas stacks releasing exhaust into the air.
A traditional Japanese Castle (城, shiro or jō), usually made from stone and wood.
A castle, in a style that can be found in France and other parts of Europe.
An emoji to depict a wedding, displayed by most vendors as a Christian church and love hearts. Some platforms display a cross or bell on the building.

The Statue of Liberty, often used as a depiction of New York City.

Due to its initial inclusion in an early Japanese emoji set, it is possible that this emoji was originally intended to represent the recreation of the Statue of Liberty located on the Odaiba island in Tokyo Bay.
A mosque building, a place of worship for followers of Islam. Shown with a domed roof and a minaret.
A Hindu temple or mandir; a place of worship for followers of Hinduism. Depicted on most platforms as a red, orange, or golden building with a tall spire.
A synague; a place of worship for followers of Judaism. Displayed with a Star of David on the front.
A cube-shaped building located at the centre of the Al-Masjid al-Haram Mosque in Mecca.

Foggy weather displayed as fog covering a bridge or cityscape, depending on the platform.

For platforms that show a bridge, the red Golden Gate Bridge is generally displayed.
A night sky with stars, depicted on major platforms as a cityscape at night.

A cityscape showing a variety of highrise buildings during the daytime. Often featuring several clouds in the sky.

See also: 🌃 Night with Stars
The sun rising over a mountain range, early in the morning.
A sun rising, early in the morning. Can be difficult to distinguish from a sunset in some versions of this artwork.
A view of city buildings as the last light disappears from the sky. An orange (or blue) glow lingers, before the stars of the night sky become visible.
A beautiful view, featuring an orange sky, with the sun setting over the buildings of a city skyline.
A lit-up bridge, shown at night.

A wooden painted horse, found on the carousel at a carnival. Faces to the left within almost all vendors' designs.

Can be used to convey fun, playfulness, or carefree enjoyment. It may also appear in contexts referencing a “carousel” of images, playing on the shared English word.

Could also be used to suggest ‘going in circles’, repeating the same thing over and over.

A previous version of Windows displayed the carousel horse facing right, which was changed to face left on Windows 10 for cross-platform consistency.

A slide with a ladder, as seen in children's playgrounds.

May be used to talk about children, parks, or playtime. May also be used metaphorically to talk about a smooth movement or action like the popular dance the electric slide or sliding into someone's DMs, usually for the purpose of flirting.

Additionally may be used in reference to something with a downward descent.
A large rotating wheel, often found at a carnival or fair.

A roller coaster in a theme park going down a dip in the ride. Three carriages can be seen with two people in each red carriage.

May be used to encapsulate the phrase "an emotional roller coaster", which refers to experiencing a series of rapidly changing and intense emotions, often in response to unpredictable or dramatic situations.

A pole spiraled with red, white, and blue stripes, as spins out front of a barbershop. Commonly used for various content concerning haircutting and hairstyling.

May also be associated with brothels in parts of Asia.
A circular ‘big top’ circus tent, with a triangle flag on top.

Ding! A call bell, as pressed at a front desk or reception to alert staff for service, such as from a concierge or bellhop (porter) to carry luggage at a hotel. Generally depicted as a golden bell on a wooden stand.

Commonly represents alerts or notifications to bring attention to important content. May also be used of various content concerning the hospitality and service industries.

Microsoft’s design previously featured a silver bell radiating yellow rays, as if ringing.

A moai, one of the famed, giant stone statues of human figures on Easter Island. Depicted as a gray stone carving of a stylized human head with a prominent brow and nose, most often facing left.

Sometimes used for various idiosyncratic purposes, such as conveying a stoic, deadpan, or silly expression. For example, this emoji is often used to represent various "sigma" or "chad" memes due to its chiselled emotionaless features.

Its official Unicode name of Moyai and inclusion in early Japanese emoji sets, such as from au by KDDI, suggest the emoji may represent the Moyai Statue near Shibuya Station in Tokyo, Japan; previous designs from Google and Microsoft resemble the Tokyo statue. Other Tokyo landmarks are represented in 🗼 Tokyo Tower and, formerly, Shibuya 109.

A steam train, powered by coal or wood. An early type of locomotive, now mostly replaced by electric or diesel trains.

May also be used figuratively to show support for a cause, trend, or movement, encouraging others to "get on board" with an idea, or to indicate that someone is joining the "hype train" or following a popular opinion or action.

A railway (railroad) car (carriage) that is generally pulled along a railway line by a locomotive. Shown with a pantograph above the carriage on many platforms which makes it look more like a tram car.

Google’s artwork previously looked like a bus and Microsoft's older versions appeared similar to a minecart.

A high speed train, designed to cover long distances at high speed.

Can be used figuratively to show support for a cause or movement, inviting others to “get on board” with the idea—much like announcing “all aboard!” when a train is about to depart.

A high-speed train, designed to cover long distances at high speed. Also features a streamlined bullet nose, often used in reference to the Shinkansen in Japan.

Can also be used figuratively to show support for a cause or movement, inviting others to “get on board” with the idea—much like announcing “all aboard!” when a train is about to depart.

A train, of no specified type. Due to the presence of a steam train and fast train emoji, this is likely to be a regular electrified or diesel passenger train.

Can be used figuratively to show support for a cause or movement, inviting others to “get on board” with the idea—much like announcing “all aboard!” when a train is about to depart.

A metro: frequent underground train found in built-up areas with high populations.

This emoji is generally displayed as a forward-facing train, with some platforms also displaying a tunnel as a circle surrounding the train. Apple's artwork shows the characters IL2 which may be a reference to one of the more locked-down buildings at Apple's Infinite Loop Headquarters during iPhone development (IL2 = Infinite Loop 2).

A form of public transport similar to a tram, but running on a track or network separated from cars and other types of traffic.

Difficult to discern from a train at small sizes.
A station, presumed to be a train station. Displays a train alongside a platform, where passengers can board.

A form of public transport on rails, usually found on streets in cities or other urban areas. For short or medium-length journeys.

Trams tend to be similar to light rail, with the difference being that they don’t tend to have their own dedicated tracks.

This emoji is generally shown as the front of the tram, on tracks. The intended usage of this emoji, instead of the tram car emoji is not clear.

Similar to a train, but running on a single track. Monorails are often found at theme parks, or other tourist destinations.

According to the designers, Facebook's design for this emoji drew inspiration from the Disneyland monorail.

A train and railway in the mountains.

Previously displayed as a funicular in Microsoft’s artwork. Android also previously displayed this train as front-facing and leaving a tunnel, which appeared similarly to the metro emoji at small sizes.

A form of public transport on rails, usually found on streets in cities or other urban areas. For short or medium-length journeys.

Trams tend to be similar to light rail, with the difference being that they don’t tend to have their own dedicated tracks.

This emoji is generally shown as the side of the tram. The intended usage of this emoji, instead of the tram emoji is not clear.
A bus used for public transport in cities and towns. Could also be used as a school bus.
The front of a bus, showing the windscreen, as well as wing mirrors in some versions of this emoji.
A type of bus that uses overhead electrical wires for power. Appears similar to a cross between a bus and a tram car.
A small bus or minivan designed to carry fewer people than a full-sized bus. Displayed in white on most platforms, though it is green on Facebook.
An ambulance, used to transport patients between their home and the hospital.

A red fire truck, an essential part of emergency services along with a police car or ambulance.

May be on the way to put out a fire.

A police car, shown with an emergency light on the top.

This emoji is displayed from the side, as opposed to the oncoming police car emoji, which is shown from the front.

A police car, shown with an emergency light on the top.

This emoji is displayed from the front, as opposed to the police car emoji, which is shown from the side.
A yellow taxicab, iconically seen in New York City. Shown from the side, as opposed to the oncoming taxi emoji.
A yellow taxicab, iconically seen in New York City. Shown from the front, as opposed to the taxi emoji which displays the side of the vehicle.

A car shown from the side, facing right-to-left. Appears as a red car on almost all platforms (which goes faster), though earlier Google designs displayed the vehicle as either silver or blue.

Facebook's first design for this emoji was also blue.

A blue or green Sport Utility Vehicle or station wagon, often with a spare tire on the back. Commonly used as a generic blue or green car.

Sport Utility Vehicle or SUV is an emoji whose meaning was likely lost in translation as it moved from Japanese phone carriers to the Unicode Standard in 2010.

This emoji goes back to the late 1990s when it was included in Docomo's emoji set. In 2009, it appeared on a proposal as one of many symbols available on Japanese phones recommended to be encoded into the Unicode Standard. In that proposal, the symbol was referred to as a "recreational vehicle" or RV. The original Japanese emojis look more like station wagons or SUVs than RVs.

At various points, platforms including Google and Samsung showed this emoji as an RV, but ultimately the designs across platforms converged to a car that looks more like an SUV or station wagon. At a small scale this emoji is barely distinguishable from 🚗 Automobile on some platforms.
A red or turquoise pickup truck. Used to talk about trucks or modes of transportation in general.
A delivery truck, most likely carrying packages of online purchases.

A large articulated lorry consisting of a tractor and a trailer connected by a pivoted bar.

Can be used to reference hauling stock for different companies and services, such as the items on sale within department stores. Also used as a dump truck for transporting materials from a dig site, both literally and figuratively.

A racing car that appears as a Formula One vehicle or rally car on most platforms. Generally displayed in red.

Apple's version of this emoji features the Swift (programming language) logo on the side.

In April 2024, WhatsApp updated its design for this emoji as part of a partnership between the messaging platform and the Mercedes-Benz F1 team.
A motorcycle, otherwise known as a motorbike used for sport/racing purposes. For a transport-based motorcycle, use a motor scooter.
A motor scooter, which may be displayed as any type of motorbike with or without a step-through frame. Distinct from the racing motorcycle, which is used for sport, not transport.

A manual wheelchair. Most platforms show a red and black or blue and black wheelchair. Distinct from ♿ Wheelchair Symbol, which is used as signage to indicate accessible facilities. See also 👩‍🦽Woman in Manual Wheelchair or 👨‍🦽Man in Manual Wheelchair.

🦼 Motorized Wheelchair was approved at the same time as this emoji.

A motorized wheelchair. Most platforms show a red and black or blue and black wheelchair. Distinct from ♿ Wheelchair Symbol which is used as signage to indicate accessible facilities. See also 👩‍🦼Woman in Motorized Wheelchair or 👨‍🦼Man in Motorized Wheelchair.

🦽 Manual Wheelchair was approved at the same time as this emoji.

An auto rickshaw, often referred to as a tuk tuk. This motorized version of a cycle rickshaw is used for transport in many regions of the world. Generally this emoji has three wheels and open sides without doors.
A bicycle, sometimes called a push bike, used for transport or sport.
A non-motorized scooter, with two wheels and handles.

A skateboard emoji, usually showing the board from the top.

Twitter's design shows the under-side of the board, as did a previous Microsoft design.

Emojipedia's sample image was modelled after Tony Hawk's skateboard.
A single vibrantly colored roller skate. Colors and styles vary across platform.

A sign indicating the location of a bus stop by the side of a road.

Some platforms display this as a red, white and blue sign which can be found in parts of Japan. This interpretation has a slight resemblance to the Pepsi Globe.

Other platforms base this emoji design on bus stop signage of other regions.

A wide road, shown from a first-person perspective. Usually shown with an overhead gantry sign providing directional guidance, though some vendors show a roadside route confirmation sign instead.

Apple's artwork displays a road sign to Curpertino, the city in California where the company is headquartered. Microsoft and Skype previously showed a sun on the horizon.

A railway track shown from a first-person perspective, as though someone is driving a train or walking down the tracks a la Stand By Me.

The track is usually surrounded by foliage and trees, sometimes with clouds in the sky and mountains in the distance. Microsoft's design previously showed the track heading directly towards a large looming mountain.

A barrel for transporting bulk liquids, such as oil. Generally depicted as a red or blue metal drum with holes or a stopper on its lid. Commonly used for various content concerning petroleum or hazardous waste.

Google’s design previously displayed a yellow oil drop symbol, while Samsung's design previously featured a yellow hazard sign.

A wheel with a rubber tire.

May be used in reference to wheels, tires, or vehicles with wheels. May also be used in expressions with 'wheel' like third wheel or hell on wheels.

A revolving red light as seen on top of police cars or other emergency vehicles. Used in emergency circumstances, often accompanied by a loud siren.

Can be used to represent emergencies, warnings, urgent alerts, or shocking disclosures.

A set of red, orange (amber) and green traffic lights, used at intersections. Less common than the vertical traffic light.

Similar in appearance to the traffic light controls in the upper-left of every OS X windows.
A set of red, orange (amber) and green traffic lights, used at intersections. More common than the horizontal traffic light.

A red, octagonal sign, often but not always shown with a white or grey rim. Used in many countries as a stop sign.

Unlike other platforms, Huawei's design for this emoji displays the word "STOP".

A sign used to indicate roadwork or construction. Generally shown as yellow and black diagonal stripes, and often used to physically block access to a road or area. May be used to imply a website or project in progress or under construction.

A round white and orange or red ring buoy with string laced through its perimeter. Also called a life preserver.

Maybe be used to talk about water, boats, and safety. May also be used metaphorically to talk about someone or something that saves.

A narrow lightweight water vessel that is usually pointed on both ends and made of either wood or plastic.

Generally depicted with a paddle.
A motorized speedboat used for recreation on lakes, or other bodies of water.
A large boat designed to carry passengers across a body of water.

A small boat powered by an engine. Also known as a speedboat or powerboat.

May be used for sexual slang.
A large ship, used for transport of people or cargo across the ocean. May be a cruise ship, commonly found around tropical locations.
A light aircraft which is shown with propellers on some platforms.
A plane taking off from a runway. Generally displayed left-right, with the front of the plane elevated.
A plane approaching a runway for landing. Generally displayed left-right, with the front of the plane facing toward the ground in a position that may result in a crash if attempted in the real world.

An open parachute floating through the air with a human steering. Most platforms feature a ram-air design. Colors vary across platforms.

Can be used to represent parachuting or skydiving, or to metaphorically represent a quick exit from an awkward or uncomfortable situation.

A seat, which could refer to any form of place to sit, with the distinction that a seat is generally fixed, and is not a chair which can be moved.

This emoji is intended to be a seat on some form of mass-transit, such as on an airplane, train or bus. Google previously displayed this as an orange wooden chair.
A helicopter, which can hover in the air. Often seen in emergency circumstances such as transporting patients to a hospital, or for police or fire-fighting activity.
Similar to a monorail, a suspension railway is elevated, but the vehicle is suspended under the track.

A cable car transportation system allowing users to swiftly ascend up a mountain. Can also be used as a tourist attraction, or as a form of public transport.

Can be mistaken for the 🚡 Aerial Tramway during that emoji's periods of viral attention.

An Aerial Tramway, most commonly seen at ski resorts, for transport between locations on a mountain. Can also be used as a tourist attraction, or as a form of public transport.

In 2018 this emoji was the focus of a grassroots campaign on Twitter (now X) where users of the platform began using this emoji more frequently. This was to update the least-used emoji on emojitracker.com (as tracked by the @leastUsedEmoji Twitter bot) from the Aerial Tramway to another emoji.

In May 2025 this emoji was also used within YouTube comments to signify laughter or approval or to create confusion for people not in the know. This was an emulation of what occurred with the 🪑 Chair emoji in 2021, which you can learn about here.
A satellite which orbits the earth, and is generally used for communications, weather, and GPS.
A rocket being propelled into space. Sometimes used to indicate a fast increase, for instance when referring to stocks going to the moon 🚀 (rising quickly in price).
A flying saucer, sometimes referred to as an Unidentified Flying Object (UFO). Previously shown on some platforms with an alien at the controls and/or a beam of light emitting from the base.

A hand waving most commonly used to say “hello” or “goodbye”.

This emoji can be used to convey a sense of not being friends any more when used on WeChat in China.
A raised hand, showing the reverse side of the palm. May be paired with the forward-facing raised hand emoji.
The palm of a hand with the fingers spread apart. Held in a manner that may indicate the number five. Similar to 👋 Waving Hand, but without any motion.
A raised hand, with the fingers separated between the ring finger and the middle finger.

An open right hand facing right, so as to show the back of the hand with the thumb on the top and the pinky on the bottom.

This emoji was developed along with 🫲 Leftwards Hand to allow for the creation of ZWJ Sequences that depict 🤝 Handshake with two different skin tone modifiers applied, one to each hand.

An open right hand facing left, so as to show the palm of the hand with the thumb on the top and the pinky on the bottom.

This emoji was developed along with 🫱 Rightwards Hand to allow for the creation of ZWJ Sequences that depict 🤝 Handshake with two different skin tone modifiers applied, one to each hand.

A hand in profile with the palm facing down.

Can be used to represent the action of dropping or reaching for something. May also be used in a variety of culture-specific contexts, including dismissal, negotiation, or as a beckoning gesture.

The design is the inverse of 🫴 Palm Up Hand.

A hand in profile with the palm facing up.

Can be used to represent the action of lifting, offering, demanding, or beckoning. May also be used to express a question or lack of knowledge.

The design is the inverse of 🫴 Palm Down Hand. The hand position is similar to the one in 💁 Person Tipping Hand.

A profile of an open hand pushing or positioned with the palm toward the left.

May be used to show a hand pushing something away or to represent rejection of something in general. May also be used with with 🫸 Rightwards Pushing Hand to show hands high fiving or holding, pressing, or squishing something.

A profile of an open hand pushing or positioned with the palm toward the right.

May be used to show a hand pushing something away or to represent rejection of something in general. May also be used with 🫷 Leftwards Pushing Hand to show hands high fiving or holding, pressing, or squishing something.

A gesture showing the index finger and thumb touching to make an open circle. Represents “I’m okay” or “yes, that’s correct / good”.

In American Sign Language (ASL), the number nine is represented with this gesture. The same hand sign can be seen as offensive in some cultures, including in parts of Europe, the Middle East, and South America.

This can also be used as a symbol of White Supremacy, depending on context.

An emoji showing the fingers held together in a vertical orientation, often referred to as the Italian hand gesture ma che vuoi, sometimes called the "finger purse." In Italy this gesture tends to be used in disagreement, frustration, or disbelief and can mean “What do you want?” or “What are you saying?” Outside Italy anyone performing a caricature of an Italian person, regardless of context or tone, might use this gesture.

Pinched Fingers has a variety of other culturally specific uses. In Israeli culture it can mean “hold on,” “relax,” or “be patient.” The K-Pop star Yuri uses it as a signature gesture to represent a dumpling and a general warm sentiment. It can also be used to represent the act of fisting.

Not to be confused with 🤏 Pinching Hand, which has overlapping senses. Both are used to represent precision when someone is making a sharp point with accompanying speech.

A hand with thumb and index finger in close proximity.

Used to suggest that something is small, or to gesture a small amount.

According to some sources, this emoji has been the subject of controversy in South Korea, following a conspiracy theory alleging that it is used primarily as an insult toward men.

A fingers crossed emoji which displays the index (first) finger crossed over the middle (second) finger. Commonly used as a gesture indicating luck, or to show desire of a favorable outcome.

This emoji was previously displayed with an additional finger on Samsung devices.

A hand with the index finger and thumb crossed and the rest of the fingers making a fist. Can be used in various contexts to represent the fingers snapping, love, or money.

In this emoji, the index finger and the thumb form a small heart shape. This gesture, used to express love or affection, is known as a finger heart and was popularized in the 2010s by South Korean celebrities, including actors, K-pop stars, and comedians.

In the context of money, this gesture may be used to indicate a luxury or an expensive item, a lack of money, or a request to be paid.

It may also be used to represent playing a tiny violin.

The gesture for “I love you” in American Sign Language (ASL), shown as a raised pinky (little) finger, index finger, and an extended thumb.

Occasionally used to represent Spider-Man’s web-shooting pose, especially when combined with the 🕷 Spider and 🕸 Spider Web emojis.
A "rock on" hand gesture raising the pinky and index fingers on one hand, which a variety of other meanings.

A hand with thumb and little (pinky) finger extended, making a traditional phone-like shape. May be used in conjunction with a face to suggest “call me” (please).

Not to be confused with the sign of the horn. Commonly used as a shaka sign, which is a similar gesture at a different orientation.

An index finger pointing to the left.

Since 2020 this emoji has been known to be combined with the 🥺 Pleading Face and the 👉 Backhand Index Pointing Right to indicate a bashful or shy pose (🥺👉👈), also often called a "simp" pose.

An alternative "simp" pose uses the  😔 Pensive Face (😔👉👈). Additionally, using the 🙄 Rolling Eyes in between the pointing finger emojis indicates a person dismissively plugging their ears in an "I'm not listening" gesture (👉🙄👈).

An index finger pointing to the right.

Since 2020 this emoji has been known to be combined with the 🥺 Pleading Face and the 👈 Backhand Index Pointing Left to indicate a bashful or shy pose (🥺👉👈), also often called a "simp" pose.

An alternative "simp" pose uses the  😔 Pensive Face (😔👉👈). Additionally, using the 🙄 Rolling Eyes in between the pointing finger emojis indicates a person dismissively plugging their ears in an "I'm not listening" gesture (👉🙄👈).

Index finger pointing upward, showing the back of the hand while doing so.

Often used to draw attention to text, a comment, or a link appearing above (‘see above’), or to emphasize agreement with a previous post (‘this,’ ‘facts’). May also be used playfully to reference oneself (‘that’s me’).

In faith-based contexts, it can signify pointing toward heaven or giving thanks to God.
A middle finger emoji, used in some western cultures as a rude or insulting gesture. The back of the hand is shown with the middle finger raised.

An index finger pointing downward, showing the back of the hand while doing so.

Generally used to highlight a piece of content placed below where this emoji can be used. This content could be a picture, a website link, or a different piece of text,

A hand with the index finger pointing straight forward at the person viewing the emoji. Used to represent the word and concept of 'you,' the second-person singular and plural pronoun.

This symbol is seen in art, advertisements, and military recruitment posters as a way to draw the viewer into the image they're looking at.

This hand shape is also used in multiple sign languages from around the world.

A thumbs-up gesture indicating approval.

In certain contexts, the thumbs-up emoji can be construed as passive-aggressive or sarcastic. Despite this possible use, it remains a popular means of quickly and earnestly expressing approval.
A thumbs-down gesture indicating disapproval.

A fist displayed in a position to punch someone, or to fist-bump another person.

It can also be used as a closed hand concealing a hidden object.

Shown as a right hand on all supported platforms. An equivalent left-handed version does not exist.
A fist pointing left, which may be used in conjunction with the right-facing fist to complete a fist-bump gesture.
A fist pointing right, which may be used in conjunction with the left-facing fist to complete a fist-bump gesture.
Two hands clapping emoji, which when used multiple times can be used as a round of applause.

Two hands raised in the air, celebrating success or another joyous event.

Originally animated to show hands being raised, as might be done along with the the exclamation Banzai! in Japan. Now more commonly only shows the hands in the air.

Two hands forming a heart shape. Used to express love and support.

This emoji currently showns the heart being made through two hands being curved into a C-shape with their thumbs touching. This is stereotypically referred to as the "Millennial Hand Heart".
Two open hands, representing openness. Sometimes used as a hug, or as a display of jazz hands.

Two hands held out together with open palms facing up, in a slightly cupped manner, as if expecting an object to be placed within them.

May also be used to represent an open book in American Sign Language (ASL), or the gesture used by followers of Islam when praying.

Two hands performing a handshake gesture, indicating a cordial greeting between friends or associates.

As of late 2021's Emoji 14.0 recommendations, this emoji design has multiple skin tone modifier options. Certain platforms did, however, support a small number of single skin tone options for the handshake emoji prior to 2021 (e.g. both Google and Samsung in 2017). View all handshake emojis.

Two hands placed firmly together, meaning please or thank you in Japanese culture. A common alternative use for this emoji is for prayer, using the same gesture as praying hands. It can also represent a respectful greeting or show of adoration many in Southeast Asian religions and cultures, such as the Hindu namaste or Buddhist añjali mudra.

Rarely used as a high-five, despite often being suggested as one by emoji keyboard search features. More about this emoji and its possible meanings.

A previous version of this emoji displayed a yellow burst of light behind the two hands on iOS. Android once showed a blob-character with closed eyes and folded hands.

Colored nail polish being applied to fingernails.

While it can be used literally in posts about beauty, glamour, or self-care, this emoji is most widely recognized for conveying confidence, sass, and a sense of nonchalance or indifference.

Shown as red, pink, or purple nail polish on most platforms, the color rarely changes the meaning of this emoji. Previously displayed as a single bottle of nail polish on Android and on Windows.
A mobile phone held up to take a selfie (photo of the person holding the phone or camera). Generally represented as a disembodied arm holding a mobile phone.

An arm flexing to show its biceps muscle. Represents strength, or working out.

Often used to highlight and celebrate “feats of strength,” whether physical, mental, or symbolic.
A mechanical or prosthetic arm.
A mechanical or prosthetic leg.
A human leg, shown detached from a human body. Displayed from the thigh and includes the foot.
A human foot shown with five toes and may include part or all of the ankle. Shown on some platforms as the sole of a foot.
A single human ear. May be used in the context of listening, or hearing something.
An ear shown with a hearing aid, worn by a person with hearing loss. The style shown in Behind The Ear (BTE), but this can represent any form of hearing aid.

A human nose. May be used to indicate smelling, or something that smells.

This emoji is considered bigoted in certain contexts, particularly when used to disparage, insult, or abuse people of the Jewish faith.

A human brain, shown in pink on most platforms. Used to indicate thinking or the human mind.

On platforms such as TikTok this emoji can have an alternative NSFW meaning.

A red anatomical heart, shown with blue or purple veins on some platforms.

Sometimes used interchangeably with ❤ Red Heart.

Pink anatomical lungs and trachea, shown with bronchial tubes on some platforms. Used in medical contexts to talk about lung health. Sometimes used in reference to taking deep breaths, hyperventilating, or breathing in general. Also used in the context of smoking or vaping.
A single tooth, like those found in your mouth. Shown as a premolar across all major emoji vendors.

A bone which may be used for a dog to chew on, or as a part of the human body. The type of bone is not specified.

May be used to represent the NSFW term "to bone".

A pair of eyes, glancing slightly to the left on most platforms. The Google version of this emoji previously showed only a single eye, despite the name of this character being eyes (plural).

Sometimes used to indicate ‘pervy eyes’ to indicate approval of an attractive photo posted online; or ‘shifty eyes’ to convey a deceitful act.

A single human eye, looking forward. This eye is in a different shape and style to the pair of eyes, which are more rounded, and looking to one side.

Notably used alongside the mouth emoji to create the "It is what it is" emoji face: 👁👄👁. Learn more here.
A tongue, sticking out. May be used as a childish sign of defiance. Alternatively: licking, in various contexts.

A human mouth which is generally displayed as a pair of lips and a top row of teeth, instead of the inside of the mouth.

May be used to indicate the spoken word or as an alternative to Kiss Mark.

Notably used alongside two eye emojis to create the "It is what it is" emoji face: 👁👄👁. Learn more here.

A mouth with the top teeth biting down on one side of the lower lip.

Used in romantic contexts to express flirtation or arousal. Can be used to express anticipation or excitement in general. Also may be used to express anxiety, pain, worry, or insecurity.
Two human footsteps,  showing the outline of both feet, including all five toes.
Google's designs for this emoji contain a subtle question mark (?).

The double helix of DNA, the genetic blueprint for life. Color and orientation vary across platforms, but positioned at a 45° angle and in multiple, bright colors to represent the molecule’s spiraling, ladder-like structure.

Can be used for various content concerning biology, genetics, and science more generally. May be used for various content concerning literal or figurative life and evolution. May also be used as sexual slang.
A red drop of blood. May be used to talk about bleeding, injury, blood donation, or menstruation.

The face of a baby with a small tuft of hair on top of its head. Some platforms show the baby sucking on a pacifier, and some platforms show a single tooth in the baby’s open mouth. Android previously displayed this emoji as a swaddled baby.

On Snapchat, the baby emoji signifies a new friend on the service. This emoji can also be used in the context of the meme “I’m baby.”

A child with no gender specified. This emoji may be used to talk about children in a gender-inclusive way.

Variants include 👧 Girl and 👦 Boy.

The face of a boy, smiling.

Previously differentiated from 👨 Man on Android by wearing a cap, and on iOS by the lack of any facial hair.

Variants include 👦 Child and 👧 Girl.

The face of a girl, smiling. Most platforms feature the girl's hair in pigtails.

Variants include 👦 Child and 👦 Boy.

An adult with no gender specified. This emoji may be used to talk about adults in a gender-inclusive way.

Variants include 👩 Woman and 👨 Man.

A person with blond hair. This emoji maintains blond hair no matter which skin tone is chosen. This emoji may be used to talk about blonds in a gender-inclusive way.

Previously displayed as a man with blond hair on all platforms, though shown as a woman with blond hair in earliest Google, Microsoft, and Samsung designs.

Variants include 👱‍♀ Woman with Blond Hair and 👱‍♂ Man with Blond Hair.
The male version of 🧑 Person.

This emoji may be used to talk about bearded people in a gender-inclusive way. It was approved in 2017, initially intended to have a male presentation. Gendered variants of this emoji were approved three years later, leading to this emoji's design being made more neutral in appearance by all major vendors.

Variants include 🧔‍♂ Man with a Beard and 🧔‍♀ Woman with a Beard, both approved in 2020.

A man shown with long hair and a beard.

A baby with a halo and wings. Can represent a sweet baby, a biblical cherub, a mythological cupid, a decorative putto, or an angel as a supernatural being in general. This emoji can be used earnestly or in a tongue-in-cheek way to talk about goodness or innocence.

It is often used to express affection for people, especially children at birth or, more sadly, after death. This emoji pops up in a large variety of contexts ranging from innocence, love, Valentine's Day, positive feelings like gratitude, and the Christian faith, especially during Christmas.
The silhouette of a person speaking. Faces left-to-right, with lines demonstrating speech being expelled. Sometimes used in the context of shouting or mansplaining.
Generic profile of one person. Often used in interface design to represent a user.
Generic profile of two people. Often used in interface design to represent users.

Two people hugging, shown as faceless blue or grey forms on most platforms. Details of each person are not distinct and thus no options are available to customize the gender or skin tone of either individual.

Not to be confused with 🤗 Hugging Face, which is less clearly a representation of hugging and sometimes used as jazz hands or to express excitement.

Has been known to be confused for a 🎥 Movie Camera emoji when displayed at small sizes, owing to similarities in shape and color.

In some cultures and religious contexts, this emoji may also be used as a sign of prayer or worship.

Earlier designs led some users to misinterpret this emoji as showing a person doing push-ups, lying down for a massage, or doing a cute "head resting on hands" gesture. While it may be used in these ways infrequently, its most common meanings are those of apology and respect.

May be used in a similar context to the acronym SMH (shaking my head), or in relation to the Picard Facepalm meme.
